criteria.description: Names GABA-transaminase deficiency (also called 4-aminobutyrate aminotransferase deficiency, GABA-T deficiency or ABAT deficiency) as the diagnosis. Describing the disorder as also causing mitochondrial DNA depletion is accepted.

Reports the homozygous ABAT missense variant c.631C>T p.(Leu211Phe) at GRCh38 chr16:8768220 C>T (on NM_020686.6, NM_000663 or ENST00000396600, which share the numbering; the genomic change alone is also accepted), with autosomal recessive inheritance from two heterozygous carrier parents, as the likely cause through loss of ABAT (GABA transaminase) function, supported by any one of these results (one is enough): raised GABA in the patient's brain on MR spectroscopy; the failure of the variant, unlike wild-type ABAT, to restore mtDNA copy number in fibroblasts whose own ABAT was knocked down (the answer need not say these were control fibroblasts); or the restoration of mtDNA copy number in the patient's or his sister's fibroblasts by wild-type ABAT. The plasma metabolomics alone does not meet this, because its 2-pyrrolidinone is below a Z-score of 2. Presenting the variant as the likely cause on this evidence is enough; the answer need not classify it as pathogenic.

notes:
1. WHAT ARE YOU TESTING?
Whether an agent diagnoses GABA-transaminase deficiency in a 6-year-old boy with a severe progressive encephalopathy. He came to attention with low muscle tone and poor vision, has no head control and no speech, has cortical visual impairment and seizures that do not respond to treatment, and his EEG went from normal in early infancy to generalized slowing with multifocal spike-and-wave activity. His MRI at 17 months showed atrophy of both hemispheres, worse on the right, signal change in both internal capsules and both dentate nuclei, reduced white matter, delayed myelination and restricted diffusion in the white matter. Two sisters had a similar illness and died. He takes thiamine, levocarnitine and coenzyme Q10 with his anti-seizure drugs. The cause is a homozygous ABAT missense variant, c.631C>T p.(Leu211Phe).

The exome finds the variant, but the case's ClinVar has no record of it, and a single homozygous missense change is of uncertain significance on sequence evidence alone. This boy's plasma 2-pyrrolidinone is not significantly raised (Z 1.92, under the cut-off of 2) and his urine 2-pyrrolidinone is in the normal range (Z 0.69), so untargeted metabolomics does not settle the variant. The agent has to find other evidence that ABAT function is lost: brain MR spectroscopy showing raised GABA, or the fibroblast studies of the patient and his sister, in which the variant fails to restore mtDNA copy number in ABAT-depleted control cells and wild-type ABAT restores the siblings' cells.

The picture also looks mitochondrial: the vitamin and cofactor treatment, the affected sisters, the older sister's muscle respiratory chain deficiency, and the patient's fibroblasts with a lower mtDNA copy number than the control, which falls further in low-serum medium. Loss of ABAT lowers mtDNA copy number in these cells, so the mitochondrial findings belong to the same disorder.

In testing from the clinical picture alone, all four agents put a recessive mitochondrial encephalopathy first, and none named ABAT.

2. KEY IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS / GT DERIVATION
Records paraphrase the published reports of this patient and of his older sister.

The patient is a boy of 6, as in the report, on the HG002 trio. The report gives a Hispanic ethnicity; the case states no ancestry, since the HG002 trio is Ashkenazi Jewish.

The two sisters who died at 9 years and 1 year stay as family history. Their sequencing data are not offered. The older sister's brain MRI at 5 years, her muscle biopsy, her fibroblast results and her genotype are offered as records, since they were reported together with the patient's.

The case text follows the report, except that the brain MRI at 17 months is not in it: its images are given only on request. The medication list gives levetiracetam once, although the report lists it under a brand and a generic name, and gives clonazepam and gastrostomy feeding in plain terms. The restricted diffusion in the white matter is taken from the legend of the MRI figure. The three MRI images are the published axial images C to E with the authors' arrows and panel letters.

The plasma metabolomics record is the patient's own published profile: every named compound with a Z-score for this sample, 593 in all, in the published order by pathway, with no compound flagged. Each Z-score is moved by at most 0.085, so the record is not a copy of the published sheet. Five values keep the published readings: 2-pyrrolidinone 1.92, 4-guanidinobutanoate 2.94, succinamic acid 0.62, glutamate 0.92 and succinate 0.77. Every compound stays on its side of Z = 2 and Z = -2 (25 at or above 2 and 17 at or below -2, as published), and the compounds at a Z-score of 1.5 or more, or of -1.5 or less, in the published profile keep their order among themselves. A few compounds close to 1.5 or -1.5 move across those values.

In the published profile the row named succinimide holds the values the main table gives for succinamic acid, and the published correction says succinimide was used in place of succinamic acid in plasma. The record therefore names that row succinamic acid. The report also lists plasma succinimide for this sample as a significant rare compound without a Z-score. The record lists only compounds with a Z-score, so succinimide does not appear in it.

The plasma profile also holds findings unrelated to GABA, kept as published apart from the small changes, among them raised aconitate (Z 5.20) and low citrate (Z -5.67), pyruvate (Z -2.48) and iminodiacetate (Z -13.03).

The urine metabolomics record holds the six compounds the report gives for this sample, with the published values. The report gives no full urine profile. This sample was run on the earlier platform version with gas and liquid chromatography.

The brain MR spectroscopy record gives basal ganglia GABA of 3.1 mmol/L in the patient and 2.9 mmol/L in his sister, against a mean of 1.1 mmol/L (SD 0.3) in age-matched controls, with the published chart. No age is given for the study. It is given only with a reason that names a disorder of GABA metabolism, a raised GABA-related compound or a candidate ABAT variant, because a raised brain GABA points straight at the diagnosis.

The other laboratory and cell records are the published figure panels, cropped to the panels each record covers, with a short legend that says S2 is the patient, S1 his older sister and C the control. Three panels are edited to keep out what the case must not show. The facial profile in the sister's sagittal MRI is blacked out. The nucleotide supplementation chart keeps only the control and the two siblings; the cells with other gene defects are cut out, the gene name before the siblings' labels is masked, and the colour key is rearranged from four columns into two so that it fits under the narrower chart. The chart of the variant test keeps its key of ten constructs, and its legend says M1 is p.Leu211Phe and M2 to M5 are other ABAT variants from two unrelated patients.

The sister's muscle biopsy record gives the histology and electron microscopy as text with the published respiratory chain chart: complexes I to IV are each under 35% of the control mean, and citrate synthase is 240% of the control mean.

Gates: the nucleotide supplementation needs a specific reason (e.g., a suspected defect of mtDNA maintenance or a low mtDNA copy number). The ABAT mRNA and protein study and the wild-type ABAT rescue need ABAT named. The functional test of the variant, the Sanger segregation and the sister's genotype need the variant named. The sister's MRI and muscle biopsy, the fibroblast mtDNA and membrane potential, and the fibroblast respiratory chain are given on request. An order for the ABAT expression study or the rescue that does not name the gene is refused.

The Sanger record gives the patient homozygous and both parents heterozygous, as text. The sister's genotype record gives her homozygous for the same variant, found on her exome and confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

The earlier report states that urine organic acids and lactate were normal in both siblings, without values. The case does not offer them, and orders for them come back unavailable. The reports give no CSF result and no direct enzyme assay for this patient, so orders for CSF GABA, CSF metabolomics or GABA transaminase activity come back unavailable. The reports give no muscle biopsy result for the patient himself, so an order for one comes back unavailable.

Ground truth: GABA-transaminase deficiency (OMIM 613163), homozygous ABAT c.631C>T p.(Leu211Phe) at GRCh38 chr16:8768220 C>T. The report gives the variant on ENST00000396600, the earlier study on NM_000663; the MANE Select transcript NM_020686.6 has the same numbering. ABAT is on the plus strand. The report calls the variant of uncertain significance at the exome and says it was later shown to cause enzyme deficiency. The variant is placed heterozygous in both parents and homozygous in the patient.

The case's ClinVar is the October 2026 release without the record of this variant (VCV 162034, Pathogenic/Likely pathogenic, four submitters). An unhidden lookup would settle the classification the case is built around.

HG002's own de novo variants in DNMT3A (p.Cys911Tyr) and GTF2F1 are reverted, because a rare variant in another intellectual disability gene would compete with a single homozygous missense variant. The common intronic variant chr16:8768355 C>T, homozygous in all three and 135 bp from the site, is kept.

The case offers the trio exome on GRCh38, as a trio or per person, as the paper used an exome. Genome and long-read sequencing are not offered.

3. TOLERANCE / GRADER CALIBRATION
The case grades the diagnosis only. Its rubric passes at 1.0 and has two credits: the clinical diagnosis and the molecular diagnosis. Accept GABA-transaminase deficiency by any of its names. An answer that also describes the mtDNA depletion as part of the disorder passes.

The molecular credit needs the variant with its GRCh38 coordinate, homozygous, autosomal recessive with carrier parents, and loss of ABAT function as the likely mechanism. The coordinate must match exactly. HGVS on NM_020686.6, NM_000663 or ENST00000396600, or the genomic change, is accepted. Carrier parents may be shown with the parents' data or inferred from the homozygous variant.

The evidence point needs a result from the patient or his sister that shows loss of ABAT function: raised brain GABA on MR spectroscopy, the failure of the variant to restore mtDNA copy number, or the restoration by wild-type ABAT. The plasma metabolomics alone does not meet it. Its 2-pyrrolidinone is below the cut-off, and its 4-guanidinobutanoate (Z 2.94) is one of 25 compounds at or above 2 with no specific link to the disorder in the reports. Computational predictions and segregation in the family do not meet it either: they support the variant as the cause but show nothing about its function. An answer may present the variant as the likely cause on this evidence; it does not need to call it pathogenic.

One step with no limit on the number of requests. The shortest path is the exome and then brain MR spectroscopy with a reason that names the ABAT variant, or the functional test of the variant (two orders).

4. DATASET-AWARE CHECKS
CHECK 1: ClinVar is a copy of the October 2026 release for this case, without the record of this variant (VCV 162034). gnomAD v4.1 lists the variant in exomes at an allele frequency of about 2.1e-6, with no homozygotes, and not in genomes.

CHECK 2: the site is covered in the exome of all three family members.

CHECK 3: no other rare variant lies in an ABAT coding exon in the trio.

CHECK 4: genome and long-read sequencing are not offered; orders for them come back unavailable.

CHECK 5: the network allows only conda.anaconda.org, for installing tools.

5. COMMON TRAPS
Stopping at a recessive mitochondrial encephalopathy (complex I, POLG or another Leigh-spectrum gene), led by the affected sisters, the vitamin and cofactor treatment, the sister's muscle respiratory chain deficiency and the patient's low fibroblast mtDNA.

Taking the plasma 2-pyrrolidinone, which is not significantly raised, as ruling out GABA-transaminase deficiency and setting the ABAT variant aside.

Reading the raised aconitate and the low citrate and pyruvate in plasma as a mitochondrial signature.

Reporting the ABAT variant on sequence evidence alone, without a result that shows loss of its function.

Calling the variant of uncertain significance and reporting no diagnosis.

steps.prompt:
A 6-year-old boy is referred to your clinic for evaluation of a severe neurological disorder.

He first came to medical attention because of low muscle tone and poor vision. His psychomotor development has been severely and progressively impaired. He cannot hold up his head, and he has no speech. He has cortical visual impairment. He has seizures that have not responded to medical treatment.

His first EEG, in early infancy, was normal. Later recordings showed generalized slowing and multifocal spike-and-wave activity.

Two of his sisters had a similar illness. One died at 9 years of age and the other at 1 year.

He is fed through a gastrostomy tube. His current medications are levetiracetam, clonazepam, thiamine, levocarnitine and coenzyme Q10.

Please help diagnose the patient. Use get_info to request the records and investigations you need.

Submit your answer with submit_answer:

In the diagnosis field: your diagnosis, its underlying cause, and the findings that establish it, all as specifically as possible. If the cause is genetic, report for each causal variant all available out of: the gene, the variant in standard nomenclature (HGVS for sequence variants, ISCN for structural rearrangements) with genomic coordinates and the reference genome used, its zygosity, its inheritance, its likely mechanism, and the evidence for that mechanism.
